name: HIV
definition: HIV is a virus that attacks the immune system and, with treatment, can be managed as a long-term condition.
overview: HIV is a virus that attacks the immune system. It is passed on through certain body fluids, and some people have a short flu-like illness soon after infection while others notice nothing for years. HIV is not the same as AIDS, which is the most advanced stage of infection. There is currently no cure, but antiretroviral treatment helps people live long, healthy lives. WHO and Terrence Higgins Trust both say that a person on effective treatment whose virus is suppressed will not pass HIV on to sexual partners.
causes: Infection with the human immunodeficiency virus, a virus that attacks the immune system.
The virus passes on when certain body fluids, such as blood, semen, vaginal fluids and breast milk, reach another person's bloodstream or mucous membranes.
It can also be passed on by sharing needles.
It can pass from a mother to her baby during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding.
riskFactors: Sex without a condom, since condoms are the most effective protection against HIV during sexual contact.
Sharing needles or other injecting equipment.
Social factors such as stigma, discrimination, income, education and where a person lives can shape risk.
Stigma and mistrust of health care can keep some people, such as people who inject drugs, from seeking testing, care and treatment.
signs: Swollen glands and a skin rash during the early flu-like illness.
Infections that are more frequent or more severe because the immune system is weakened.
complications: Opportunistic infections, which happen more often or are more severe when the immune system is weakened.
A greater chance of becoming ill with diseases such as tuberculosis, other infections and some cancers.
AIDS, the most advanced stage, in which failure of the immune system allows life-threatening infections and cancers to take hold.
Passing HIV on to a baby during pregnancy, delivery or breastfeeding, a chance that effective treatment lowers.
diagnosis: HIV is diagnosed with a test, which the NHS provides free of charge to anyone. Testing can be done at a sexual health clinic, with a home testing kit or with a home sampling kit. A clinic may offer a finger-prick test with results in minutes, while a more detailed test can take a few days. If a first test suggests HIV, a further blood test confirms the result. A test may not pick up HIV acquired very recently, a gap called the window period, and its length differs between tests. Early diagnosis means treatment can start sooner.
treatment: HIV is treated with antiretroviral medicines, which stop the virus from replicating in the body. These are taken every day as the doctor recommends, and the aim is an undetectable viral load. Terrence Higgins Trust says treatment is recommended straight away and still protects the immune system when it has already been damaged. Treatment is free on the NHS in England.
prevention: Condoms are the most effective protection against HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. PrEP is medicine taken by people without HIV to lower their chance of acquiring it, and it is free through NHS sexual health services. PEP is a short course of medicine taken after a possible exposure. Not sharing needles also helps prevent HIV. Effective treatment prevents onward transmission, including to sexual partners.
seekCare: Anyone who thinks they have recently been exposed to HIV can go to a sexual health clinic or an A&E department, where PEP is available, and the sooner it is started the more likely it is to work. A routine HIV test is available free from NHS sexual health services, or with a home kit. Terrence Higgins Trust's helpline, THT Direct, can connect people with an HIV doctor. Someone who is seriously unwell can call NHS 111, or 999 in an emergency.

references.title: World Health Organization: HIV and AIDS fact sheet

sections.heading: What is HIV, and is it the same as AIDS?
sections.body:
HIV is a virus that attacks the immune system. HIV and AIDS are not the same thing: HIV is the virus, while AIDS is the most advanced stage of infection. Without treatment, infection moves through an early acute stage and a chronic stage before reaching AIDS. The CDC says progression to AIDS is less common today because of advances in treatment. An NHS hospital HIV service says most people living with HIV will never develop AIDS, because effective treatment stops the virus progressing in this way.

There is currently no cure for HIV. It can be treated with antiretroviral medicines, and WHO describes it as a manageable long-term condition when prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care are available.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of HIV?
sections.body:
Some people have a short flu-like illness around 2 to 6 weeks after acquiring HIV, according to the NHS. It can include a sore throat, a high temperature, swollen glands, muscle aches, tiredness and a skin rash. The CDC says this illness may last a few weeks. Other people have no symptoms in the first few weeks after infection.

After this early phase, HIV may cause no symptoms for many years, although the NHS says the virus keeps damaging the immune system during that time. This is one reason an early diagnosis matters: treatment can then start sooner, which can improve the chances of controlling the virus. WHO says HIV makes it easier to become ill with tuberculosis, other infections and some cancers.

sections.heading: How is HIV passed on?
sections.body:
HIV is passed on when infected body fluids get into another person's bloodstream, the NHS says. WHO lists blood, breast milk, semen and vaginal fluids as the fluids involved. The CDC explains that these fluids must reach a mucous membrane or damaged tissue, or be injected directly into the bloodstream. The NHS adds that HIV can be spread by sharing needles. It can also pass from a mother to her baby during pregnancy and delivery and through breastfeeding, and effective treatment lowers the chance of this.

HIV does not spread through the air like cold and flu viruses, the NHS says. WHO states that casual contact such as kissing or sharing food does not spread it, and the NHS describes passing it on through kissing alone as extremely rare.

sections.heading: How is HIV diagnosed?
sections.body:
HIV is diagnosed with a test, and the NHS provides testing free of charge to anyone. Options include testing at a sexual health clinic, a home testing kit and a home sampling kit. With a home testing kit a person collects a saliva sample or a small spot of blood and tests it themselves, whereas with a home sampling kit the sample is posted to a laboratory. If a first test suggests HIV, a further blood test is needed to confirm the result.

A test may not detect HIV acquired very recently, a gap known as the window period, and its length differs between tests. It is still possible to pass on HIV during the window period.

sections.heading: What treatment is available, and what does undetectable mean?
sections.body:
HIV is treated with antiretroviral medicines, which stop the virus from replicating in the body. These are taken every day as the doctor recommends, and the aim is an undetectable viral load. NHS 111 Wales says most people taking daily treatment reach an undetectable viral load within about six months, and Terrence Higgins Trust says it can take up to six months for some. Terrence Higgins Trust says treatment is recommended straight away and still protects the immune system when it has already been damaged.

Terrence Higgins Trust says someone on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load cannot pass on HIV, and WHO says a person on treatment who is virally suppressed will not pass HIV to sexual partners. This is often shortened to U=U, meaning undetectable equals untransmittable. The Trust adds that a current sexually transmitted infection does not change this.

sections.heading: How can HIV be prevented?
sections.body:
The NHS says condoms are the most effective protection against HIV and other sexually transmitted infections. PrEP, or pre-exposure prophylaxis, is medicine taken by people without HIV to lower their chance of acquiring it. It is available free through NHS sexual health services, usually as tablets taken daily or on demand, although some people may need an injection. PrEP does not protect against other sexually transmitted infections, so condoms are still advised.

PEP, or post-exposure prophylaxis, is a short course of medicine after a possible exposure to HIV. It is available from sexual health clinics and A&E departments, and the sooner it is started the more likely it is to work. The CDC advises never sharing needles, syringes or other drug injection equipment.

sections.heading: Living with HIV
sections.body:
Terrence Higgins Trust says people living with HIV can now have long, healthy lives. An NHS sexual health service describes near normal life expectancy with treatment. HIV services in England are open access, so adults with a diagnosis can refer themselves to a provider of their choice.

Support goes beyond medical care. Terrence Higgins Trust offers counselling, face to face or online, and a helpline, THT Direct. It also runs peer support in which everyone taking part is living with HIV, including a group for people recently diagnosed or finding it hard to come to terms with a diagnosis. Other community organisations listed by an NHS trust include Positive East and Positively UK.

faqs.q: Is HIV the same as AIDS?
faqs.a: No. HIV is a virus, while AIDS is the most advanced stage of HIV infection. The CDC says progression to AIDS is less common today because of advances in treatment. An NHS hospital HIV service says most people living with HIV will never develop AIDS, because effective treatment prevents the virus progressing in this way.

faqs.q: Can a person with HIV pass it on if they are on treatment?
faqs.a: Terrence Higgins Trust says someone on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load cannot pass on HIV. WHO says a person on antiretroviral treatment who is virally suppressed will not pass HIV to sexual partners. This is known as U=U, undetectable equals untransmittable. Condoms still protect against other sexually transmitted infections.

faqs.q: Can HIV be passed on by kissing or sharing food?
faqs.a: WHO states that casual contact such as kissing or sharing food does not spread HIV. The NHS says the virus does not spread through the air like cold and flu viruses, and that passing it on through kissing alone is extremely rare. It is passed on when infected body fluids get into the bloodstream.

faqs.q: Is there a cure for HIV?
faqs.a: There is currently no cure for HIV. It can be treated with antiretroviral medicines, which stop the virus from replicating. With access to effective prevention, diagnosis, treatment and care, WHO describes HIV as a manageable long-term condition that lets people live long and healthy lives.

faqs.q: Where can someone get tested for HIV?
faqs.a: The NHS provides HIV testing free of charge to anyone, including at sexual health clinics. Home testing kits and home sampling kits are also available. If a first test suggests HIV, a further blood test confirms the result. Early diagnosis means treatment can start sooner.
